title: Subperiosteal Orbital Abscess (SPA): Clinical Mastery
summary: A critical ophthalmic emergency characterized by purulent collection between the periorbita and the bony orbital wall, usually secondary to paranasal sinusitis. Rapid recognition and the 'Garcia Criteria' are essential for determining medical vs. surgical intervention to prevent vision loss and intracranial extension.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Subperiosteal Abscess (SPA) is an accumulation of pus between the periorbita and the orbital bone. It most commonly occurs along the medial orbital wall (lamina papyracea) due to ethmoid sinusitis. While historically managed surgically, modern management often permits conservative medical therapy in select pediatric populations under strict monitoring. It represents Stage III of the Chandler Classification of orbital infections.

rows: Eyelid edema, no proptosis, full motility
Proptosis, chemosis, limited motility, no abscess
Pus between bone and periorbita; globe displacement
Pus within orbital fat/soft tissues; severe ophthalmoplegia
Bilateral signs, CN III/IV/VI palsies, systemic sepsis

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Exophthalmos (Proptosis): Usually non-axial (displaced away from abscess)
Pain: Exacerbated by eye movement
Eyelid Edema & Erythema: Often tense and 'woody'
Ophthalmoplegia: Limited extraocular motility (EOM)
Chemosis: Bulbar conjunctival edema
Decreased Visual Acuity: Sign of optic nerve compression or ischemia
Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD): Late/Critical sign

sections.title: Surgical Red Flags: Immediate Drainage Required
content: Decreased visual acuity (VA) or new RAPD
Proptosis > 5mm or worsening proptosis
Intracranial extension (meningeal signs, altered mental status)
Abscess volume > 1mL or width > 4mm on CT
Frontal sinus origin (higher risk of intracranial spread)
No improvement after 24-48 hours of IV antibiotics

content.explanation: Management without surgery is viable if: 1. Age < 9 years. 2. Medial location. 3. Small size (<0.5-1ml volume). 4. Absence of visual compromise or RAPD. 5. Absence of frontal sinusitis. 6. Rapid clinical response within 24-48 hours.

rows: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis (Single aerobe common)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: Clinical Assessment (Vision, Pupils, Motility, IOP, Color Vision)
Step 2: Contrast-Enhanced CT (Gold Standard): Look for lenticular-shaped collection
Step 3: MRI Orbit/Brain: If suspecting intracranial spread or cavernous sinus thrombosis
Step 4: Laboratory: CBC with diff, Blood cultures, CRP/ESR
Step 5: Nasal Endoscopy: Performed by ENT to assess sinus status and culture

sections.title: Step-by-Step Management Protocol
content: 1. Admission: Mandatory for IV antibiotics and serial q4-q6 hour vision checks.
2. Empiric IV Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone (100mg/kg/day) + Vancomycin + Metronidazole (for anaerobes).
3. Corticosteroids: Consider IV Dexamethasone after 24-48h of coverage to reduce orbital inflammation.
4. Nasal Decongestants: Oxymetazoline spray to facilitate sinus drainage.
5. Surgical Intervention: If red flags are present or Garcia criteria are not met.
6. Transition to PO: Switch to oral (e.g., Augmentin or Clindamycin) after 48h afebrile and clinical improvement.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques
content: Endoscopic Endonasal Drainage: Preferred for medial abscesses; avoids external scars; allows simultaneous sinus surgery.
Lynch Incision (External): Traditional approach for superior/medial abscesses; 2cm curvilinear incision between inner canthus and nasal bridge.
Transcaruncular Approach: Minimally invasive medial access.
Lateral Canthotomy/Cantholysis: Immediate bedside decompression if orbital compartment syndrome is present.

rows: Painful, good response to steroids, no fever/sinusitis
Rapid onset proptosis in children, mass on imaging
History of slowly growing painless lump
Tender swelling over the lacrimal sac, epiphora

sections.title: Potential Complications
content: Ocular: Permanent vision loss from CRAO or Compressive Optic Neuropathy
Orbital: Exposure keratopathy, EOM fibrosis/permanent strabismus
Intracranial: Meningitis, Epidural/Subdural abscess, Brain abscess
Vascular: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (High mortality rate)
Systemic: Septicemia, Osteomyelitis of the frontal bone (Pott's Puffy Tumor)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Tips
content: Always check color vision and saturation; it often fails before Snellen acuity.
A medial abscess typically displaces the globe down and out.
Superior/Frontal abscesses have a much higher risk of intracranial extension than medial ones.
If a patient's vision is dropping, do not wait for the CT to finish—consider decompression.
Non-medial SPA (superior or inferior) almost always requires surgical drainage regardless of age.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent meta-analyses (e.g., Wong et al.) support the 'Medical First' approach for pediatric medial SPA < 1mL. There is an increasing trend toward early Endoscopic Endonasal Drainage (EED) which reduces hospital stay compared to medical management alone. Multidisciplinary care involving Ophthalmology, ENT, and Pediatrics is now the gold standard of care.
